assessments.quote: 23. Working with Instruments and Effects
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: Every track in Live can host a number of devices. These devices can be of three different sorts:
assessments.assessment: Three common device sorts are documentary context; no device-count/resource bound is supplied.

assessments.quote: MIDI effects act upon MIDI signals and can only be placed in MIDI tracks.
assessments.assessment: MIDI effects require MIDI tracks. RCK006 is one valid ordered chain, not an exhaustive common-track eligibility/invalid-drop case.

assessments.quote: Audio effects act upon audio signals and can be placed in audio tracks, return tracks, and the Main track. They can also be added to MIDI tracks as long as they are placed after an instrument.
assessments.assessment: Audio effects can occur on audio/return/Main and after a MIDI instrument. Existing ordered MIDI chain is true; separate common audio/return/Main placement actions are missing as-of original61.

assessments.quote: Instruments receive MIDI and output audio; they can be placed in MIDI tracks.
assessments.assessment: Instrument on MIDI track and MIDI-to-audio role are represented by actual instrument insertion RCK048; no synth/output model follows.

assessments.quote: To learn about a particular device and how to operate it, consult the Live Audio Effect Reference, Live MIDI Effect Reference, or Live Instrument Reference chapters.
assessments.assessment: Reference links route individual device operation elsewhere; no entire reference chapter or device DSP was read/adopted here.

assessments.quote: To learn about creating and using custom groupings of instruments and effects, check out the Instrument, Drum and Effect Racks chapter.
assessments.assessment: Rack grouping reference is separately audited124-block primary source; this full153-block common chapter is a different scope.

assessments.quote: Further information about track types in Live can be found in the Routing and I/O chapter, including information on using return tracks to distribute the effect of a single device amongst several tracks.
assessments.assessment: Routing/track-type/return-distribution chapter reference only. No full Routing chapter or case coverage is borrowed here.

assessments.quote: You can get hands-on with devices by assigning their parameters to MIDI or key remote control.
assessments.assessment: MIDI/key assignment is a routing reference, not a mapping codec, controller protocol or claim of missing generic mapping actions.

assessments.quote: 23.1 Device View
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: The Device View is where you insert, view, and adjust the devices for a selected track. You can double-click a track’s title bar to view its devices in the Device View, which appears at the bottom of Live’s window.
assessments.assessment: Actual existing track-title double-click opens Device View. Do not confuse track-title entry with device-title folding or insertion.

assessments.quote: By default, either the Device View or the Clip View can be used at a time depending on whether a device or clip is in focus. If you want to tweak device parameters and edit notes or samples without switching between views, you can stack the Clip View above the Device View.
assessments.assessment: Existing Clip View clause and actual Toggle-with-DeviceView action already cover stacking; either-view default is source context, not a new constructor/history law.

assessments.quote: Use the toggles next to the Clip and Device View Selectors in the bottom-right corner of Live’s window to expand both views.
assessments.assessment: Existing actual opening-route/Toggle case covers Clip selector/toggle stacking; no false missing generic stack action.

assessments.quote: You can also use the keyboard shortcuts CtrlAlt3 (Win) / CmdOption3 (Mac) to show or hide the Clip View and CtrlAlt4 (Win) / CmdOption4 (Mac) to show or hide the Device View.
assessments.assessment: Clip shortcut is represented. Source Device show/hide CtrlAlt4/CmdOption4 is distinct from existing Alt/Option4 focus; add that explicit Device hide/show history without aliasing focus or clip opening.

assessments.quote: To save space in the Device View, a device can be collapsed by double-clicking its title bar or by choosing Fold from the title bar’s context menu.
assessments.assessment: Device-title double-click and context Fold are explicit collapse entries absent from selected common Rack actions; track-title double-click is a different already-owned entry.

assessments.quote: 23.2 Using Devices
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: Live’s devices can be accessed in the browser. The browser’s sidebar contains labels for built-in devices, Max for Live devices, and third-party plug-ins.
assessments.assessment: Browser labels for built-in/Max/plug-ins are source access context; RCK048 truly loads a browser instrument. Does not prove all host formats/eligibility.

assessments.quote: The easiest way to place a device in a track is to double-click it in the browser, which adds it to the selected track or creates a new track if one is not selected. Alternatively, select a destination track by clicking within it, then select a device or preset in the browser and press Enter to add it to the selected track.
assessments.assessment: Enter on a selected destination is genuinely covered. Double-click with selected versus no selected track and actual destination click are separate missing common insertion contexts.

assessments.quote: You can also drag devices into tracks or drop areas in the Session and Arrangement Views, or into the Device View. Dragging a sample to the Device View of a MIDI track creates a Simpler instrument with this sample loaded.
assessments.assessment: Sample into empty MIDI Device View genuinely creates Simpler under existing factory-dropping precondition; selected-sample custom defaults differ. Session/Arrangement/drop-area/DeviceView device drag routes need explicit actions, not new codec laws.

assessments.quote: If you want to use an external input signal to feed a track in Live, the track’s Arm button in the mixer must be activated in order to hear the input through the devices in the track’s device chain when using the default Auto monitoring setting. On MIDI tracks, this is normally activated automatically when inserting an instrument.
assessments.assessment: External input under Auto/arm belongs to existing monitoring matrix. Normally automatic MIDI-instrument arm is already an explicit new/empty/unarmed/ExclusiveArm U probe, not a universal constructor or false missing action.

assessments.quote: This is how you would play live instruments through effects on a track, for example, or use a MIDI keyboard’s input to play a track’s instrument. You can easily move from this setup into recording new clips for further use in a Set. If you have alternative monitoring preferences, please see the Monitoring section to learn how to configure these settings.
assessments.assessment: Live-through/recording guidance refers to Monitoring. Existing productive input/clip matrix is real; no new record-success/default/latency law.

assessments.quote: To add another device to the track, simply drag it there or double-click its name to append it to the device chain. Signals in a device chain always travel from left to right.
assessments.assessment: Left-to-right flow and valid ordering are represented. Double-click append to an existing chain is a distinct missing entry; no universal insertion index beyond source context.

assessments.quote: You can drop audio effects in at any point in an audio track’s device chain, keeping in mind that the order of effects determines the resulting sound. The same is true for a MIDI track’s device chain.
assessments.assessment: Order-dependent processing is source role, not numeric composition. Audio-chain effect insertion can be sampled on valid contexts without all incompatible relocation semantics.

assessments.quote: If you drop an instrument into a MIDI track’s device chain, be aware that signals following (to the right of) the instrument are audio signals, available only to audio effects. Signals preceding (to the left of) the instrument are MIDI signals, available only to MIDI effects. This means that it’s possible for a MIDI track’s device chain to hold all three types of devices: first MIDI effects, then an instrument, and finally audio effects.
assessments.assessment: Existing actual MIDI-effect→instrument→audio-effect chain covers the valid signal-type order; do not invent rejected-drop/load repair outcomes.

assessments.quote: To remove a device from the chain, click on its title bar and press your computer’s Backspace or Delete key, or select Delete from the Edit menu. To change the order of devices, drag a device by its title bar and drop it next to any of the other devices in the Device View. Devices can be moved to other tracks entirely by dragging them from the Device View into the Session or Arrangement Views.
assessments.assessment: Generic selected-device edit actions already exist through NAV079 and clause024. Explicit title-select Delete/Backspace versus Edit Delete, title drag within DeviceView and cross-track Session/Arrangement drops need entry-specific common probes.

assessments.quote: Edit menu commands such as cut, copy, paste, and duplicate can be used on devices. Pasted devices are inserted in front of the selected device. You can paste at the end of a device chain by clicking in the space after the last device, or by using the right arrow key to move the selection there. Generally, devices can be placed, reordered, and deleted without interrupting the audio stream.
assessments.assessment: RCK049 genuinely pastes before selected device and at clicked empty end; NAV079 actually Cut/Copy/Paste/Duplicate/Delete. Right-arrow selection of chain end and explicit menu routes remain narrow gaps. Generally uninterrupted audio is qualified, not a continuity guarantee.

assessments.quote: Devices in Live’s tracks have input and output level meters. These meters are helpful in finding problematic devices in the device chain: low or absent signals will be revealed by the level meters, and relevant device settings can then be adjusted, or the device can be turned off or removed.
assessments.assessment: Named input/output device meters aid diagnosis; no common Rack case inspects both with genuine signal/bypass controls. Calibration/detector/refresh and inference from silence remain U.

assessments.quote: Note that no clipping can occur between devices because there is practically unlimited headroom. Clipping can occur when an overly strong signal is sent to a physical output or written to a sample file.
assessments.assessment: Practically unlimited internal headroom/clipping advice remains source research; no numeric range, internal precision, guaranteed no-clipping or output/file clipping model is adopted.

assessments.quote: After reading about using devices in Live, you might find it interesting to look into clip envelopes, which can automate or modulate individual device parameters on a per-clip basis.
assessments.assessment: Clip-envelope automation/modulation is an owner reference only; not an imported complete evaluator/timebase or new device automation case.

assessments.quote: 23.2.1 Device Title Bar
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: The controls in a device’s title bar can be used to activate or deactivate the device, save and hot-swap presets, create defaults, and open the device’s context menu.
assessments.assessment: Activator and existing swap/save-cancel actions are genuine subsets. Default creation and actual device Options/context entry are separate gaps, not implied by title-bar presence.

assessments.quote: Certain title bar controls are only available for some devices, such as the scale awareness toggle for devices that can follow a clip’s scale, and the Learn toggle for the Chord device.
assessments.assessment: Scale-awareness and Chord Learn controls are explicitly conditional per-device contexts; route individual behavior to device owners. No universal toggle, available-device set or feature closure from name.

assessments.quote: Devices are turned on or off using their Activator toggles.
assessments.assessment: RCK050 actually turns an audibly processing audio effect off. This is the real existing bypass action, not an all-instrument/whole-Rack output law.

assessments.quote: Turning a device off is like temporarily deleting it: the signal remains unprocessed, and the device does not consume CPU cycles. Live devices generally have no impact on CPU usage unless they are active. For more information, please refer to the Managing the CPU Load section. The Freeze Track command discussed there is especially helpful when working with CPU-intensive devices.
assessments.assessment: Audio-effect bypass qualitative subset is already represented. CPU-zero/generally-active language and Freeze reference remain research/other-owner; no performance/sample/tail guarantee or disabled-instrument audio result.

assessments.quote: Some devices have views that you can expand above the Device View, such as the Gain Stage and Modulation Matrix sections in Roar and the Frequency Display in EQ Eight.
assessments.assessment: Roar Gain Stage/Modulation Matrix and EQ Eight Frequency Display are source examples of above-DeviceView expansion; actual named offered view controls need selected device-owner reconciliation, not all-device availability.

assessments.quote: Devices with this kind of view have an arrow toggle to the right of the Activator toggle. Use the toggle to show or hide the view.
assessments.assessment: Arrow to right of Activator toggles above-view display for eligible devices; missing explicit generic entry action, with real eligibility/visible baseline first.

assessments.quote: Some views can also be expanded within a device itself, for example, the LFO and Envelope Follower sections in Phaser-Flanger. This kind of view is indicated by a triangle icon in the device title bar.
assessments.assessment: Triangle title icon distinguishes within-device expansion, with Phaser-Flanger LFO/Envelope Follower examples. Separate from the arrow/above-view case and from uninspected pixels.

assessments.quote: A context menu is available for every device and contains general editing commands such as Cut, Copy, and Rename. Some commands are unique to a particular device, such as the Mono Sidechain option in Auto Filter.
assessments.assessment: Cut/Copy generic operations already exist; Rename and device-specific Mono Sidechain are contextual menu examples. Do not adopt Auto Filter behavior through a generic menu or claim every command shared.

assessments.quote: You can right-click a device’s title bar or use the Show Options toggle to open the context menu.
assessments.assessment: Actual device-title right-click and Show Options toggle are two explicit context-menu entries; add bounded route actions rather than merely asserting menu presence.

assessments.quote: 23.2.2 Device A/B Comparison
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: Every built-in Live device includes two device states, A and B, which can store separate parameter values. This lets you save and compare the changes you make when creating or editing presets. You can save an iteration of a preset that you don’t want to overwrite to one device state and continue experimenting on the other.
assessments.assessment: Two A/B parameter-value states of built-in devices are explicitly outside current common clause026. Eligible non-Rack built-in context must be independently established; no DSP/state codec.

assessments.quote: Using device states to compare parameter settings can also be useful for things like EQing and compression, where minor adjustments can make a noticeable difference. You can try out slight parameter variations to hear how they affect the resulting sound or check the changes against default values.
assessments.assessment: EQ/compression comparison advice supplies no audible-difference threshold or promise any parameter change is detectable; genuine productive effect needed in future sound comparisons.

assessments.quote: When a device is first loaded, its default parameter values are used for both A and B. Once you adjust a parameter, B retains the initial values, and any changes you make only apply to A.
assessments.assessment: First-loaded values in both slots and later A edits retaining B are documented history, not a solved source of every factory/custom/default value. Need genuine distinguishable parameter states and matched initialization context.

assessments.quote: To copy the current parameter values from the A device state to B, select the Compare: Copy A to B command from the Edit menu, the device’s context menu, or its Show Options toggle.
assessments.assessment: Compare: Copy A to B is explicitly offered in Edit, device context and Show Options routes. Actual copy actions need source-qualified states; not generic clipboard or inverse-command label guesses.

assessments.quote: You can switch from the A device state to B using the Compare: Switch to B command or the P key. When the B device state is selected, a “(B)” appears next to the device’s name in the title bar.
assessments.assessment: Compare: Switch to B or P, plus literal (B) title indicator, are explicit A→B entry roles. Keyboard focus/platform conflicts remain U; no unshown reverse label is invented.

assessments.quote: The Compare commands are available for both device states, so how you save parameter values to A and B is up to you. You could use one device state to keep the default values as a reference, or use both states to design completely different-sounding presets. Note that these commands are not available for Racks, Max for Live devices, or plug-ins.
assessments.assessment: Commands are available for both states; Racks/Max/plug-ins excluded. Advice about defaults versus different sounds is not exact default/DSP proof; unsupported-device negatives need eligible productive baseline.

assessments.quote: Because A and B are unique device states, any parameter automation you create in one state is not shared with the other. This means if you automate a parameter in the A device state, that automation will be disabled when you switch to B and is not automatically re-enabled when you switch back to A.
assessments.assessment: Automation is state-specific: switching disables, and returning does not automatically re-enable. Needs actual productive active parameter automation before the switch, not just stored envelope presence.

assessments.quote: To reactivate any disabled parameter automation, use the Re-Enable Automation command in the parameter’s context menu when the device state you want to use is selected.
assessments.assessment: Parameter-context Re-Enable Automation with intended state selected is distinct from global/transport re-enable. Actual command after genuinely disabled automation is missing as-of common owner.

assessments.quote: This command can be used from either device state. Keep in mind that since automation is specific to A and B, it will be disabled again each time you switch from one state to the other.
assessments.assessment: Either-state re-enable and disable again on each subsequent switch are separate histories. No automatic restoration on returning or universal envelope/evaluator law is chosen.

assessments.quote: Only the parameter values from the selected device state are copied or duplicated. For example, if you copy a device while A is selected, the new device will use the parameter values from the original’s A device state for both A and B, even if the original’s B device state has other values.
assessments.assessment: Generic actual copy/duplicate operations are represented elsewhere but not A/B selected-state semantics. Copy while A and separately B selected, then inspect both slots of new instance; preserve original distinct other slot.

assessments.quote: Similarly, if you save a preset to your User Library, the parameter values from the selected device state are used for both A and B.
assessments.assessment: Saving preset uses selected slot for both A/B. Need successful owned save/load and selected A versus B histories; RCK052 only cancels save, not this slot reconstruction.

assessments.quote: Note that device states can be accessed via the Live API with Max for Live.
assessments.assessment: Exact selected API direct members retain can_compare_ab condition/12.3 source availability and target U. API roles/actions are not UI A/B case credit, API-call execution, UI/API parity or scheduling/message proof.

assessments.quote: 23.2.3 Live Device Presets
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: Live devices can store and retrieve their parameter settings as presets. Each device appears in the content pane of the browser as a folder that can be opened to reveal its presets.
assessments.assessment: Device preset folders and load/store roles are present generally; browser folder opening and actual default-versus-custom preset choice need explicit selected-context actions.

assessments.quote: The folder represents the default preset for a device; this can be either the original factory settings or a custom default you have saved. The presets within the folder have custom settings. Presets are included as part of the Core Library and Packs. You can also create and save your own presets.
assessments.assessment: Parent folder denotes factory OR saved custom default; Core Library/Pack/user presets remain distinct. Default folder cannot universally mean factory settings or exact preset bytes.

assessments.quote: You can browse and load presets quickly with the computer keyboard:
assessments.assessment: Keyboard browse introduction is an actual entry family; next three list items provide the concrete gestures.

assessments.quote: Scroll up and down using the up and down arrow keys.
assessments.assessment: Up/down preset navigation is separate from actual load; do not convert selection into load unless explicit admitted Options context.

assessments.quote: Close and open device folders using the left and right arrow keys.
assessments.assessment: Left/right folder close/open is an explicit browse gesture; no exhaustive browser selection/focus grammar.

assessments.quote: Press Enter to load a preset onto a selected track.
assessments.assessment: Existing Enter-load action truly loads onto selected track. Preset formats/state remain separate unknowns.

assessments.quote: You can also double-click a preset in the browser to load it onto a selected track, or drag and drop a preset from the browser onto a track’s title bar or device chain.
assessments.assessment: Actual preset double-click and drag to track-title/device-chain are distinct finite routes beyond current Enter case; matched successful admitted preset needed.

assessments.quote: Note that it is generally recommended to load presets via the browser; however, it is also possible to drag Live-specific device file types (such as .adg, .adv, and .amxd) directly into a Live Set from the Explorer (Win) / Finder (Mac).
assessments.assessment: Browser recommended but OS Explorer/Finder direct .adg/.adv/.amxd drops are permitted context. No arbitrary extension acceptance, parser/ABI/codec or OS drag support proof from names/link.

assessments.quote: If you want to replace a preset on a track with a different one, you can drag and drop a new preset from the browser and place it over the existing preset in the track’s device chain.
assessments.assessment: Dropping a preset over existing chain preset is explicit replacement entry, separate from moving a device or HotSwap exit; retain successful original/load baselines and no media/undo atomicity law.

assessments.quote: 23.2.4 Hot-Swapping Presets
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: Using Hot-Swap mode is a quick way to replace a preset on a track. In this mode, the preset on the track is linked to the browser so that you can audition and load different presets. To start hot-swapping, press Q or click the Hot-Swap Presets button in the device’s title bar.
assessments.assessment: Existing case enters HotSwap, loads compatible preset and Esc exits; add explicit Q and title HotSwap Presets button entries and matched audible audition context without numeric identity.

assessments.quote: If you press Q to enter Hot-Swap mode, the currently selected preset on the track will be made available for swapping. If no preset is selected, the first audio effect (on audio tracks) or the instrument (on MIDI tracks) will be swapped.
assessments.assessment: Q targets selected preset, otherwise first audio effect on audio or instrument on MIDI. These distinct selection/no-selection histories are missing; eligibility/context productive first.

assessments.quote: Once Hot-Swap mode is enabled, the preset is selected in the browser and its device folder is expanded. You can replace the preset with another one from the same folder or navigate to a different folder to swap in a preset for another device. Only presets of the same device type can be hot-swapped. For example, it is not possible to swap an audio effect for a MIDI effect.
assessments.assessment: Compatible loading already true; preset-selected/browser-folder-expanded and same/different folder navigation need explicit action. Same device-type does not imply every preset accepted or cross-type replacement supported.

assessments.quote: Use the up and down arrow keys to navigate through the presets. Press Enter to load the selected preset or double-click the preset you want to load. If you want to use a device’s default settings, select the device’s parent folder and load that instead of one of its presets.
assessments.assessment: Actual arrows then Enter/double-click and loading parent-folder default are separate HotSwap roles; loaded parent may be custom default, never presumed factory.

assessments.quote: Note that you can automatically load presets in Hot-Swap mode by adding the -EnableHotSwapOnSelection entry to the Options.txt file. With this option, the existing preset is replaced as soon as a new one is selected in the browser.
assessments.assessment: Literal -EnableHotSwapOnSelection is source configuration context. No Options file is changed/executed here; ordinary selection≠load without independently valid recognized option and productive loading baseline.

assessments.quote: Once you are done replacing presets, you can exit Hot-Swap mode with any of the following actions:
assessments.assessment: Exit list introduces five explicit routes. Esc already real; other entries should not imply restoring pre-load preset.

assessments.quote: Press the Q key.
assessments.assessment: Q exit needs actual admitted HotSwap state and known successful load baseline, separate from Q entry.

assessments.quote: Press the Esc key.
assessments.assessment: Esc exit after successful compatible load is already actual RCK051; no rollback expectation is added.

assessments.quote: Click the X button in the Hot-Swap bar at the top of the browser’s content pane.
assessments.assessment: Browser HotSwap-bar X is explicit exit entry; no save/cancel or rollback law.

assessments.quote: Click the X button in the device’s title bar.
assessments.assessment: Device-title X is a separate exit entry, not the same control location as browser X.

assessments.quote: Navigate from the browser to a different view.
assessments.assessment: Navigate from browser to another view exits HotSwap; source does not equate focus-only movement with every view transition or undo a loaded preset.

assessments.quote: 23.2.4.1 Hot-Swapping Samples
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: In addition to replacing entire presets, you can swap out loaded samples in Drum Rack pads, Drum Sampler, Impulse, Sampler, and Simpler.
assessments.assessment: Sample swapping names five supported contexts: Drum pad/Drum Sampler/Impulse/Sampler/Simpler. Generic preset swapping does not cover them or their sample-load formats.

assessments.quote: To do so, use the Hot-Swap Sample button that appears in the following locations:
assessments.assessment: HotSwap Sample button is distinct from HotSwap Presets and opens a sample target; following list gives qualified location roles.

assessments.quote: Drum Rack pads — At the bottom right of each pad.
assessments.assessment: Drum pad sample button bottom-right requires hover context from B083; multi-chain/unsupported pad eligibility is not invented.

assessments.quote: Drum Sampler — At the bottom right of the Waveform Display.
assessments.assessment: Drum Sampler Waveform Display bottom-right sample swap requires relevant hover and valid loaded sample.

assessments.quote: Impulse — At the bottom right of each sample slot.
assessments.assessment: Impulse per-sample-slot bottom-right button is distinct target; establish actual loaded slot before comparison.

assessments.quote: Sampler — At the top left of the Zone Editor when it is expanded.
assessments.assessment: Sampler top-left Zone Editor button requires expanded editor and is always visible in that context, exception to hover-only behavior.

assessments.quote: Simpler — At the bottom right of the Sample Display.
assessments.assessment: Simpler bottom-right Sample Display button needs relevant hover, not generic device-title preset button.

assessments.quote: Note that the button is only visible when you hover over the relevant area (except in Sampler, where it is always visible). For example, you can hover over the Waveform Display to access the button in Drum Sampler.
assessments.assessment: Hover visibility has explicit Sampler exception. Need actual before/hover/away histories on eligible loaded devices; no pixel/RGB/hitbox oracle.

assessments.quote: Clicking the button opens the folder where the sample is located in the browser. From there, you can replace the loaded sample with another one from the same folder or swap it with a sample from a different folder. Press Enter to load a selected sample or double-click the sample you want to load.
assessments.assessment: Actual sample button opens source folder; replacement via same/different folder and Enter/double-click are separate steps. No sample bytes, effects preservation or source-loss law.

assessments.quote: When you’re ready to stop swapping samples, you can exit Hot-Swap mode by:
assessments.assessment: Sample exit list has five routes; preserve its button action distinct from preset device-title X exit.

assessments.quote: Clicking the Hot-Swap Sample button in the device.
assessments.assessment: Clicking device HotSwap Sample button exits sample swap after genuine entry; no rollback.

assessments.quote: Clicking the X button in the Hot-Swap bar at the top of the browser’s content pane.
assessments.assessment: Sample browser-bar X exit is distinct from pressing a device-title preset X.

assessments.quote: Pressing the Esc key.
assessments.assessment: Sample Esc exit is source role but current RCK051 is preset context, not proof of this sample target action.

assessments.quote: Pressing the Q key.
assessments.assessment: Sample Q exit needs actual sample-HotSwap target; not inferred from selection-only preset context.

assessments.quote: Navigating from the browser to a different view.
assessments.assessment: Browser-to-other-view exits sample swap; view entry/focus distinctions remain source-scoped and no general dispatch law.

assessments.quote: 23.2.5 Saving Presets
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: You can save any presets that you have created or edited to the User Library in the browser. This makes it easy to organize and store presets for later use.
assessments.assessment: User Library preset save is represented as capability and cancellation action. Successful save/confirmation still needs actual independently writable owned destination.

assessments.quote: Click the Save Preset button in the device title bar to save the current device settings, along with any custom text you have added to the Info View, as a new preset.
assessments.assessment: Save Preset title button stores settings plus custom Info View text. Existing cancel case does not establish successful custom-text retention; exact preset codec/grammar U.

assessments.quote: Once you click the button, the browser opens (if it is closed), and the preset is highlighted in its corresponding folder in the Presets folder of the User Library. You can rename the preset or keep its default name, then press Enter to confirm the save. Alternatively, press the Esc key to cancel the process.
assessments.assessment: Browser opens/highlights correct User Library preset; actual Enter confirm versus actual Esc cancel are distinct. Esc already real; default naming and disk atomicity stay U.

assessments.quote: You can also save presets to any folder within the Places section of the browser by dragging the device via its title bar and dropping it into the desired folder.
assessments.assessment: Places title-drag save is a real documented route but lacks a common device actual action. Project selected export/collection cases retain their true narrower predicates, not exact device serialization.

assessments.quote: Note that if the Collect Files on Export option in Live’s Library Settings is set to Ask, a dialog appears asking if you want to copy the files whenever you save or drag a preset that contains referenced samples to the browser.
assessments.assessment: Ask collection dialog for sample-bearing preset is already owned by selected Project export actions. Copy/cancel ordering and atomicity retain existing scope; no duplicate whole file transaction.

assessments.quote: For detailed information on what can be done with the browser, check out the Working with the Browser chapter. For more on how to store Project-specific presets, see the Projects and Presets section in the Managing Files and Sets chapter.

assessments.quote: 23.2.6 Defaults
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: You can create custom defaults to save and apply the settings you use the most for certain devices and workflows. Defaults allow you to:
assessments.assessment: Custom defaults introduction gives four qualified families, not a universal constructor override for every asset or device.

assessments.quote: Load devices with pre-defined parameter values.
assessments.assessment: Predefined device parameter defaults need actual saved/recognized default histories, not merely folder presence.

assessments.quote: Load VST and Audio Units plug-ins with specific parameter configurations.
assessments.assessment: Plug-in default family is source context; later B118 qualifies configurations as parameter-list only, not retained values. Existing configured-instance save case is not default creation.

assessments.quote: Create new MIDI and audio tracks with specified device and mixer settings.
assessments.assessment: New audio/MIDI track default family is not existing default-Set/template behavior; explicit track default save/create actions remain missing as-of original61.

assessments.quote: Customize the presets used for sample dropping, slicing, and converting audio to MIDI.
assessments.assessment: Sample dropping/slicing/conversion presets are separate default families, not one generic preset-load operation.

assessments.quote: All defaults are stored in the Defaults folder in the User Library.
assessments.assessment: User Library Defaults folder name/entry is already owned. Actual default recognition/application/removal is not proved by BC040 folder inspection.

assessments.quote: Once a default is saved, its settings are automatically applied whenever it is used in a Set.
assessments.assessment: Saved default applies when its corresponding item is used. Requires independently recognized successful saved default first; does not give universal precedence outside later Project context.

assessments.quote: To remove a saved default, use the Delete option from its context menu in the User Library, or select the item in the browser and press the Delete key. Once removed, the factory settings are once again applied for the corresponding item.
assessments.assessment: Delete via User Library context or selected browser Delete restores corresponding factory settings. Actual saved-default application baseline before removal required; no cleanup/rollback/default-factory byte law.

assessments.quote: 23.2.6.1 Default Presets
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: Each Live device loads with its factory settings when added to a track. You can save a device with a set of specified parameter values as a default preset so that the device loads with those settings instead.
assessments.assessment: Factory initial device versus custom parameter default is explicit conditional history. Earlier factory Rack/sample-drop cases keep their matching no-custom-default prerequisites.

assessments.quote: To do so, set the desired parameter values for a device, then select the Save as Default Preset option from the device title bar’s Options menu or context menu. This option is available for all of Live’s instruments, MIDI effects, audio effects, and Rack types.
assessments.assessment: Save as Default Preset via Options/context is explicit for Live instruments/MIDI/audio effects/Rack types. No equal eligibility for Max/plug-ins inferred from all-Live wording.

assessments.quote: After the option is selected, the device is saved to the relevant folder within the Defaults folder: Audio Effects, Instruments, or MIDI Effects.
assessments.assessment: Default device-type destination Audio Effects/Instruments/MIDI Effects is visible source role; no undocumented path expansion or file encoding.

assessments.quote: You can also drag the device from a track into one of the device type folders to save it as a default preset. Make sure the preset has the original device name (e.g., Simpler) and not a unique name; otherwise, the preset will not be recognized as a default.
assessments.assessment: Drag into type folder recognizes original device name, not unique preset name. Need actual productive correct-name control before wrong-name absence; no name grammar/case/extension law.

assessments.quote: Once the preset is saved, its settings are loaded any time you add the device to a track. If you save a default for an instrument that contains a sample, the sample is also loaded.
assessments.assessment: Saved default settings reload, including an instrument-contained sample. Genuine recognized saved/default-loaded baseline first; no byte-equality, source copying or every failure outcome.

assessments.quote: If you create a new default for a device that already has one, a dialog appears asking if you want to overwrite the existing preset.
assessments.assessment: Existing-default overwrite dialog requires a genuinely saved recognized default and actual second save; choices/atomicity/cancel effects unknown.

assessments.quote: 23.2.6.2 Default Plug-in Configurations
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: You can save the parameter configuration for a VST or Audio Units plug-in as a default. Add the parameters you want to include in Configure Mode, then select the Save as Default Configuration option in the device title bar’s Options menu or context menu.
assessments.assessment: Configure list plus Save as Default Configuration Options/context route is distinct from existing Set persistence. Need actual admitted published parameter list, not arbitrary plug-in parameter discovery.

assessments.quote: The default is saved to its respective folder, either Audio Units or VSTs, in the Plug-In Configurations folder, which is automatically created the first time you save a default configuration.
assessments.assessment: AU versus VST configuration subfolder and first-save parent creation are source roles; clean owned first-save history needed, no OS path/codec law.

assessments.quote: If you have both the VST and Audio Units version of the same plug-in installed, you can create separate default configurations for each type.
assessments.assessment: Same plug-in AU and VST versions can have separate configurations; independently supported actual versions required, not cross-format binary identity/parity.

assessments.quote: Note that plug-in defaults do not retain any parameter values: only the parameters that have been added to the device panel in Live are saved. If you want to retain the parameter settings along with the configuration, add the plug-in to a Rack and then save that Rack as a default preset.
assessments.assessment: Configuration defaults save exposed parameters only, explicitly not parameter values. Rack default is recommended workaround for retaining values; do not promise all opaque plug-in DSP state.

assessments.quote: 23.2.6.3 Track Defaults
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: With track defaults, you can load devices and certain mixer settings (such as I/O routing, volume, pan, and sends) any time you create a new audio or MIDI track.
assessments.assessment: Track defaults contain devices and certain mixer settings including I/O/volume/pan/sends. Exact all-fields/all-plugin preservation is not supplied.

assessments.quote: Set up a track with the devices and mixer settings you want to store, then select the Save as Default Audio Track or Save as Default MIDI Track option from the track title bar’s context menu.
assessments.assessment: Save as Default Audio Track/MIDI Track from track-title context is explicit, separate from device preset or default Set.

assessments.quote: This saves the default to its respective folder, either Audio Track or MIDI Track, in the Creating Tracks folder in the User Library. You can also drag an audio or MIDI track into its corresponding folder to save it as a default. Note that the saved track must be named either Default Audio Track or Default MIDI Track in order for it to be recognized as a default.
assessments.assessment: Creating Tracks Audio/MIDI folders and exact source Default Audio Track/Default MIDI Track names qualify drag recognition; no broader filename codec.

assessments.quote: The saved default’s devices and mixer settings are then populated any time you create its corresponding track type.
assessments.assessment: Creating corresponding track after actual saved recognized default is the productive action; no source-independent constructor or hidden mixer state law.

assessments.quote: 23.2.6.4 Sample Dropping Defaults
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: You can specify which instrument is added when dropping a sample either into the Device View for an empty MIDI track or onto a Drum Rack pad.
assessments.assessment: Factory sample-drop subsets are true, but user can choose instrument for empty MIDI DeviceView versus Drum pad. Distinct custom-default destinations prevent unconditional Simpler/default inference.

assessments.quote: To do so, add an empty Sampler or Simpler device to a MIDI track and adjust its settings as needed. Then, drag the device into one of the two Dropping Samples folders: On Device View or On Drum Rack.
assessments.assessment: Empty Sampler OR Simpler configured then dragged into On Device View or On Drum Rack establishes explicit custom sample-drop recipe; no sample payload preloaded or arbitrary instrument acceptance.

assessments.quote: You can also save a default for Drum Rack pads via the Save as Default Pad option from a pad’s context menu, which adds the preset to the On Drum Rack folder as well.
assessments.assessment: Pad context Save as Default Pad also saves to On Drum Rack. Actual pad-default route differs from a device Default Preset command.

assessments.quote: Note that while it is possible to add multiple presets to the same sample dropping folder, only one default can be used at a time. When dropping samples, the preset that was last added to the folder is used.
assessments.assessment: Only one sample-dropping default active; last added wins even if folder has multiple presets. Needs independently productive distinct defaults and known addition order, not timestamp/filesystem sort inference.

assessments.quote: 23.2.6.5 Slicing Defaults
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: In addition to the built-in slicing presets, you can set up a custom Drum Rack for slicing audio to MIDI.
assessments.assessment: Custom slicing Drum Rack is source workflow; existing chooser case007 in conversion primary is not template creation, nor absence of future owner changes.

assessments.quote: Add an empty Drum Rack to a MIDI track, then drag an empty Sampler or Simpler device onto a pad to create a single chain. You can add any MIDI or audio effects to the chain, as well as assign device parameters to the Drum Rack’s Macro Controls. Once you have all the settings configured, drag the Drum Rack into the Slicing folder.
assessments.assessment: Empty Drum Rack plus empty Sampler/Simpler on pad, optional MIDI/audio effects and real macro mappings, then Slicing-folder drag is explicit recipe. No required exact macro layout or voice algorithm.

assessments.quote: Saved slicing presets can then be selected from the Slicing Preset chooser that appears in the Slice to New MIDI Track dialog.
assessments.assessment: Actually created valid saved slicing preset appears/selects in Slice dialog. Existing template presence sources do not establish this save/recognition chain.

assessments.quote: 23.2.6.6 Converting Audio to MIDI Defaults
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: Similar to slicing presets, you can set up custom Racks for converting Harmony, Melody, or Drums to MIDI.
assessments.assessment: Common source custom conversion defaults qualify primary chapter factory piano/synth Rack roles. Original14/29 as-of context only; no claim later owner lacks new default qualifications.

assessments.quote: It is recommended to use an Instrument Rack for the Harmony and Melody conversions, that way you can add MIDI and audio effects to the device chain. However, it is also possible to use a single instrument on its own if desired. The Drums to MIDI conversion requires a Drum Rack with Sampler or Simpler devices on its pads.
assessments.assessment: Harmony/Melody recommend Instrument Rack but allow a single instrument. Drums requires Drum Rack with Sampler/Simpler pads. No forced Rack/preset/sound for custom pitched defaults.

assessments.quote: Add the devices you want to use to the Instrument Rack (if using one), or add the drum hits you want included in the Drum Rack. Adjust the device parameters and map them to the Macro Controls as needed. Drag the configured device or Rack into one of the three Audio to MIDI folders: Drums to MIDI, Harmony to MIDI, or Melody to MIDI to save it as a default.
assessments.assessment: Configure devices/macros then drag into separate Drums/Harmony/Melody to MIDI folders; future actual save/default use requires valid assets and productive conversion, not folder presence.

assessments.quote: You can also drag an existing device or Rack preset into the conversion folders instead of creating one from scratch. Make sure to only add a Drum Rack to the Drums to MIDI folder, and not a Drum Rack nested in an Instrument Rack; otherwise, the preset will not be recognized as a default.
assessments.assessment: Existing presets may be dragged, but Drums default must be plain Drum Rack, not Drum Rack nested in Instrument Rack. Correct productive recognized baseline required before nested-preset nonrecognition.

assessments.quote: After the default is saved, it will be used any time you run its corresponding conversion command.
assessments.assessment: Saved corresponding default is used for conversion; factory/no-custom baseline must qualify original piano/synth previews. No guarantee conversion returns nonempty notes for every valid input.

assessments.quote: Note that while it is possible to add multiple presets to the same conversion folder, only one default can be used at a time. When running the conversion command, the preset that was last added to the folder is used.
assessments.assessment: Multiple conversion presets allowed in folder, only one used: last added. Addition-order history, not date/name sort or arbitrary default priority, must be independently known.

assessments.quote: 23.2.6.7 Project-Specific Defaults
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: In addition to creating program-wide defaults, you can also save Project-specific ones. This can be useful if you need specialized device or workflow settings for a particular Set but don’t want to overwrite the more general defaults you use on a regular basis.
assessments.assessment: Project-specific versus program-wide defaults are separate contexts; no generic global-library precedence outside documented Project use.

assessments.quote: To store Project-specific defaults, add a separate Defaults folder to the Current Project folder, along with any of its related folders that you want to use. You can create these folders directly in the Project folder in Explorer (Win) or Finder (Mac), or use the New Folder context menu option for the Current Project in the browser. Once created, you can drag custom devices or tracks into their corresponding folders.
assessments.assessment: Create Project Defaults/related folders in OS or Current Project New Folder then drag owned devices/tracks. Explicit folder setup, not automatic support for arbitrary names or malformed folders.

assessments.quote: It is not possible to drag a plug-in into the Current Project folder, so there is a workaround for saving Project-specific plug-in configurations. Make sure to first create the Plug-In Configurations, Audio Units, and VSTs folders in the Defaults folder for the Current Project.
assessments.assessment: Plug-in cannot be directly dragged into Current Project; create Plug-In Configurations/AU/VSTs folders first. Supported positive library configuration needed before this scoped negative.

assessments.quote: You can then save a configuration as normal and drag the plug-in folder with the Default.appc file from the User Library into the Audio Units or VSTs folder in the Current Project. Since this removes the configuration from the main Defaults folder, you can save the same default again if you also want a copy in the User Library, or create a new one with different settings.
assessments.assessment: Save library configuration then drag its Default.appc-containing plug-in folder to Project AU/VST folder; source says library copy removed and can be saved again. No Default.appc codec, arbitrary copy/move equivalence or failure atomicity.

assessments.quote: Once the Project-specific defaults are set up, they will be loaded instead of the ones from the Defaults folder in the User Library any time you use their corresponding items in a Set from the Project.
assessments.assessment: Configured Project defaults override User Library for corresponding items in that Project. Need genuinely different recognized defaults and matched in/out-Project contexts, not universal global precedence.

assessments.quote: Note that the context menu options for saving defaults are specifically for storing presets in the Defaults folder in the User Library, and therefore cannot be used to save Project-specific defaults.
assessments.assessment: Context Save Default commands specifically target User Library and cannot save Project-specific defaults; actual Project folder-drag positive route precedes no-effect comparisons.

assessments.quote: 23.3 Device Delay Compensation
assessments.assessment: Exact numbered heading/ancestry only; no behavioral or leaf completion from structural presence.

assessments.quote: Live automatically compensates for delays caused by built-in devices and plug-ins, including those on the return tracks. These delays can arise from the time taken by devices to process an input signal and output a result. The compensation algorithm keeps Live’s tracks in sync while minimizing delay between the player’s actions and the audible result.
assessments.assessment: Existing compensation scope/control and independent dry/delayed/return signal probes are real. Sync/minimal delay are goals, not measured alignment, plugin report contract or algorithm.

assessments.quote: Device delay compensation is on by default and does not normally have to be adjusted in any way. To manually turn latency compensation on (or off), use the Delay Compensation option in the Options menu.
assessments.assessment: Documented on-by-default Options Delay Compensation and actual off/on/fresh/saved case already owned; no new default-history assertion.

assessments.quote: When Delay Compensation is on, the Reduced Latency When Monitoring option is available in the Options menu. This option toggles latency compensation on and off for tracks which have input monitoring on. When enabled, input-monitored tracks will have the lowest possible latency, but may be out of sync with some other tracks in your Set, such as Return tracks, which are still delay compensated. When disabled, all tracks will be in sync, but input-monitored tracks may have higher latency.
assessments.assessment: Existing option availability and input-monitor/return separate signal histories are genuine. Lowest possible/in-sync language supplies no zero-latency/success guarantee.

assessments.quote: Note that tempo-synced effects and other devices that get timing information from Live’s internal clock may sound out of sync if they are placed in a device chain after devices which cause delay.
assessments.assessment: Existing RML055 genuinely uses characterized tempo-synced effect after qualifying delayed device. No missing generic clock interaction, phase or audible-artifact oracle.

assessments.quote: Unusually high individual track delays or reported latencies from plug-ins may cause noticeable sluggishness in the software. If you are having latency-related difficulties while recording and playing back instruments, you may want to try turning off device delay compensation; however, this is not normally recommended. You may also find that adjusting the individual track delays is useful in these cases, but please note that the Track Delay controls are unavailable when device delay compensation is deactivated.
assessments.assessment: Actual Track Delay units/availability with compensation off is already observable RML054, not private research. Sluggishness/turn-off advice supplies no numeric latency/CPU or recommendation guarantee.

assessments.quote: Note that device delay compensation can, depending on the number of tracks and devices in use, increase the CPU load.
assessments.assessment: CPU may increase with tracks/devices is conditional resource guidance; no scheduler, benchmark, complexity or utilization guarantee.
